# μMap proximity labeling in living cells reveals stress granule disassembly mechanisms

**Authors:** Chenmengxiao (Roderick) Pan; Steve D. Knutson; Sean W. Huth; David W. C. MacMillan

**Affiliations:** 1Merck Center for Catalysis at Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA | 2Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ, USA

## Abstract

Phase-separated condensates are membrane-less intracellular structures comprising dynamic protein interactions that organize essential biological processes. Understanding the composition and dynamics of these organelles advances our knowledge of cellular behaviors and disease pathologies related to granule dysregulation. In this study, we apply microenvironment mapping with a HaloTag-based platform (HaloMap) to characterize intracellular stress granule dynamics in living cells. After validating the robustness and sensitivity of this approach, we then profile the stress granule proteome throughout the formation and disassembly and under pharmacological perturbation. These experiments reveal several ubiquitin-related modulators, including the HECT (homologous to E6AP C terminus) E3 ligases ITCH and NEDD4L, as well as the ubiquitin receptor toll-interacting protein TOLLIP, as key mediators of granule disassembly. In addition, we identify an autophagy-related pathway that promotes granule clearance. Collectively, this work establishes a general photoproximity labeling approach for unraveling intracellular protein interactomes and uncovers previously unexplored regulatory mechanisms of stress granule dynamics.

Cellular processes are compartmentalized into various structures, including membrane-less organelles formed through liquid–liquid phase separation. These droplet-wise condensates are composed of both nucleic acid and protein constituents and are found to have key roles in regulating gene expression, stress responses and signaling networks1,2. Among these phase-separated condensates, stress granules (SGs) are the subject of substantial interest as they transiently associate in response to cellular stresses and, through underexplored mechanisms, dynamically disassemble when the stressor is removed3. Current evidence suggests that SGs not only serve to temporarily store and protect certain mRNAs and proteins during stress conditions4 but also profoundly impact RNA processing5,6, organelle function 7,8 and overall cell fate9,10. In addition, dysregulation of condensate organization has been linked to several neurodegenerative pathologies11,12. These include Parkinson’s13, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)14, and Charcot–Marie–Tooth15 diseases, all of which exhibit abnormal inclusions in patient’s neurons that share SG features, suggesting an association with undermined clearance of these originally transient structures. Therefore, understanding SG dynamics can reveal important fundamental principles of cellular organization as well as facilitate new therapeutic development.

While substantial efforts have revealed the biophysical and molecular principles underlying SG phase-separated formation16–18, our understanding of cell-based mechanisms for resolving SGs is comparatively limited. SG disassembly is believed to involve various post-translational modifications (PTMs)19, including phosphorylation20, SUMOylation21, glycosylation22 and ubiquitination23,24. In particular, ubiquitination was previously shown to be involved in heat shock-induced SG disassembly23. Granule composition and dynamics have also been found to be highly stress-specific25, and whether a similar mechanism exists in other granule types, including those triggered by disease-related oxidative stress26 or other environmental stimuli, remains unknown.

Despite the importance of understanding granule dynamics, studying these transient condensates remains a substantial challenge. Phase-separated structures lack membranes and are variable in shape and size, rendering traditional separation methods ineffective at isolating and studying these droplets27,28. In addition, granule composition is highly dynamic throughout formation and disassembly, and fully characterizing this changing proteome requires techniques with high levels of spatiotemporal fidelity. Proximity labeling has recently emerged as a versatile and robust methodology for studying such transient protein–protein interactions25,29–31. This technique typically involves genetically fusing a protein of interest with a catalyst that can locally generate reactive probes to covalently tag and catalog nearby interactors32. We reasoned that the microenvironment mapping (μMap) technology recently developed in our laboratory would be effective for profiling intracellular condensate compositions33. μMap does not require the use of H2O2 or the generation of singlet oxygen species34,35. It uses blue light-induced energy transfer from iridium (Ir) photocatalysts to biotin–diazirine probes to generate highly reactive carbenes, resulting in a high-resolution labeling radius (<4 nm) that is ideal for studying granule interactome changes36. Already, μMap has been successfully applied for profiling various cell surface microenvironments33,37,38, intracellular small-molecule drug targets39,40 and oncogenic chromatin states from isolated nuclei41. Using μMap within intact, live cells would offer unique insights into the nature of the intracellular proteome and condensate dynamics.

The work described herein extends the μMap platform by combining a genetically encodable methodology based on haloalkane dehalogenase (HaloTag)42 that allows the installation of a cell-permeable Ir catalyst onto intracellular proteins of interest. Using this HaloTag-based μMap platform (HaloMap), we address the underexplored mechanisms surrounding SG disassembly by targeting Ras GTPase-activating protein-binding protein 1 (G3BP1) to map the SG interactome throughout formation and disassembly (Fig. 1a). Based on this time-resolved HaloMap proteome profiling and following biochemical validation, our findings support protein ubiquitination as a key factor in SG disassembly. Subsequent HaloMap profiling of SGs under intact or impaired global ubiquitination further reveals a highly conserved homologous to E6AP C-terminus (HECT) ubiquitin E3 ligase family as a critical modifier of granule clearance, ostensibly functioning through ubiquitination of specific granule proteins. We further identify the autophagy-related ubiquitin receptor toll-interacting protein (TOLLIP) as a putative interactor with the polyubiquitinated SG proteins, leading to autophagy-assisted granule disassembly. Taken together, this work demonstrates the robustness and generality of HaloMap for revealing dynamic intracellular interactome changes, from which we identify new modulators governing SG kinetics that hold promise in advancing neurodegenerative disease research.

## Results

### HaloMap captures SG proteome

To establish the HaloMap platform for granule profiling, we first stably expressed a HaloTag–G3BP1 fusion protein in HEK293 cells. We verified that this construct adopted subcellular localization and capacity to form stress-induced granules identical with endogenous G3BP1 (Extended Data Fig. 1a). In parallel, we appended the cell-permeable μMap Ir catalyst, previously reported for intracellular TargetID39, with a polyethylene glycol(PEG)4-hexyl chloride ligand to enable covalent alkylation to the HaloTag enzyme (Fig. 1a). Ir conjugation with HaloTag is efficient under mild conditions (5 μM, 1 h)39 with minimal cellular toxicity observed (Extended Data Fig. 1b). We next combined this workflow with several media washes to remove any unbound Ir, followed by the introduction of biotin–diazirine probes for subsequent blue light photoactivation to label proximal proteins (Fig. 1b). To induce granule formation, oxidative arsenite stress (AS; 500 μM NaAsO2) was applied in parallel with biotin–diazirine probe 30 min before irradiation. Via immunofluorescence, we verified the colocalization of biotinylation signals with the cytosolic granule structures of HaloTag–G3BP1 when AS was applied, indicating high-resolution proximity labeling of these phase-separated structures (Fig. 1c). Notably, we also verified that the HaloMap workflow did not induce granule formation in the absence of NaAsO2 stress, indicating minimal interference on native cellular state (Fig. 1c).

We next examined the performance of HaloMap on AS-induced granule labeling with quantitative proteomics. After live-cell labeling, biotinylated proteins were enriched from cell lysate using streptavidin beads, followed by digestion and characterization via quantitative label-free liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) analysis. Meanwhile, this workflow was also performed in HEK293 cells stably expressing HaloTag fused to a nuclear export signal (HaloTag–NES) to account for any background cytosolic labeling (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Using this comparison, we identified 371 putative G3BP1 interactors (log2(fold change) > 0.5, P < 0.05) as stress-induced granule candidates (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Data 1). These interactors showed substantial overlap with previously cataloged SG proteins, and the most highly enriched candidates (NUFIP2, UBAP2L, CAPRIN1, etc.) have been consistently identified as core structural components of granules (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d)25,27,29,30. These results serve to validate the accuracy of our approach and corroborate previous studies concerning the composition of AS-induced granules. However, several of the identified interactors were not previously known to colocalize with granules (Fig. 1d). These include large ribosomal subunit protein L4 (RPL4), which has only been found to interact with G3BP1 during native conditions43. Additionally, we identified pumilio homolog 3 (PUM3), which is homologous to known SG components PUM1 and PUM2, as well as endoplasmic reticulum chaperone protein, protein disulfide-isomerase A6 (PDIA6). As further validation, we confirmed via immunofluorescence that these interactors localize to SGs upon AS (Fig. 1e).

G3BP1 and several related SG proteins have also been suggested to pre-associate into submicroscopic assemblies under normal conditions30,44. We hypothesized that HaloMap could also profile these prestress interactions. We compared the native interactome of HaloTag–G3BP1 against a HaloTag–NES control in the absence of stress (native (NT)) and identified 14 highly enriched (log2(fold change) > 2, P < 0.05) proteins, including USP10, G3BP2, FXR2 and YTHDF3, among others (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Data 1). These interactors have been postulated to form ‘preseed’ complexes with G3BP1 that likely underlie the quick formation of the SGs and are in close agreement with the ‘preseed’ interactors previously identified via peroxidase-based proximity labeling (Supplementary Data 1)30. Together, these findings demonstrate that intracellular HaloMap can efficiently and accurately capture both native and stress-induced G3BP1/SG interactomes.

### HaloMap identifies a ubiquitin-mediated disassembly pathway

With the HaloMap labeling platform established, we next sought to profile proteomic changes occurring during active SG disassembly to capture possible key modulators during this process. SGs fully disassemble after about 2 h of recovery in fresh media, as indicated by both live-cell confocal imaging (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and fixed-cell immunofluorescence (Fig. 2a)16. Based on these kinetics, we performed HaloMap labeling of the granule proteome at 30 min disassembly (D30), 60 min disassembly (D60) and 120 min disassembly (D120) postremoval of AS to represent the early, middle and late disassembly stages (Fig. 2b). Enriched granule interactors (n = 698, log2(fold change) > 0.5, P < 0.05) drawn from comparisons between the HaloTag–G3BP1 to HaloTag–NES labeling at each time point (Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Data 2) were assembled into a heatmap illustrating their enrichment level changes during granule disassembly (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Data 2). Unsupervised clustering showed distinct temporal patterns of both protein recruitment and depletion from the G3BP1/SG interactome, a general observation shared with a previous study30. As granules disassembled, we expected the number of labeled proteins to decrease, and indeed the enrichment of ~70% of these granule interactors decreased throughout recovery (Fig. 2c). However, we were intrigued by a distinct set of proteins (n = 203) that exhibited increasing association throughout recovery, as these may be active mediators of granule disassembly (Supplementary Data 2). Gene ontology (GO) analysis of these targets yielded a notable enrichment for proteins that positively regulate or initiate translation (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2c), supporting previous assumptions that the release of mRNAs from granules and resumption of translation occur as cells recover from stress45,46. Additionally, multiple proteins implicated in ubiquitination and protein quality control pathways were also enriched (Fig. 2c), suggesting that these PTMs may govern and participate in SG recycling. Although previous studies have also identified a potential link in this area, the precise relationship between ubiquitination and granule dynamics is not well understood24,47,48. A strong piece of evidence favoring ubiquitin-mediated SG dynamics was derived from heat shock-induced granules, where the upregulation of G3BP1 polyubiquitination potentially primes these transient structures for rapid disassembly23. Given this precedent, we questioned if ubiquitination also mediates the disassembly of SGs triggered by oxidative stress.

To begin our investigation, we first assessed whether overall ubiquitination levels increase upon AS and/or spatially associate with SGs. Via immunofluorescence, we observed strong colocalization of ubiquitin signals with that of G3BP1/granules following stress treatment (Fig. 2d), indicating these condensates contain polyubiquitinated proteins. Furthermore, we confirmed upregulation of global polyubiquitin levels upon stress and during early recovery (30 min poststress) in total cell lysate, as illustrated in a previous study49, as well as streptavidin-enriched HaloMap-labeled lysate reflecting G3BP1 interactors (Fig. 2e). To further understand the impact of ubiquitination on granule kinetics, we next tested condensate formation and disassembly in the presence of TAK-243 (MLN7243), a potent ubiquitin-activating enzyme (UAE) inhibitor that globally suppresses ubiquitination (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 2d)50. In separate groups, we inhibited ubiquitination (1) before and throughout a complete cycle of granule formation and disassembly (TAK-243-1), (2) during granule formation (TAK-243-2) and (3) for the disassembly period alone (TAK-243-3; Fig. 2g). Results from these comparisons showed that stalled ubiquitination during any period (groups 1, 2 or 3) exerted a minimal impact on granule formation, confirming similar observations that this PTM is not required for phase separation47 (Extended Data Fig. 2e). However, a considerable delay of granule disassembly was observed when ubiquitination was inhibited during granule formation (TAK-243-1 and TAK-243-2), and a minor delay was observed when TAK-243 was dosed solely during disassembly (TAK-243-3; Fig. 2h). Together, these results strongly indicate that ubiquitin PTMs are key for granule disassembly and that installation likely occurs before actual granule clearance. We hypothesized that oxidative SGs are proactively ‘prepared’ in this manner for eventual disassembly upon returning to favorable conditions.

### HaloMap identifies disassembly-related ligases and receptors

Our initial HaloMap profiling of the entire disassembly process highlighted several ubiquitin-related proteins (Fig. 2c), and we observed a substantial delay in granule disassembly kinetics upon TAK-243 treatment (Fig. 2h). Given these data, we were next interested in identifying specific ubiquitin-related mediators that may facilitate granule clearance. These likely include ubiquitin E3 ligases that catalyze polyubiquitin PTMs onto specific protein substrates, presumably during granule formation (Fig. 2d,e,h), as well as ubiquitin receptors that may recognize these PTMs during disassembly23,48. Despite the overall success of our temporal HaloMap experiment, which yielded results consistent with other proximity labeling methods used previously to profile granule composition25,29,30, it remains particularly challenging to distinguish ubiquitin ligase–substrate interactions from the granule protein networks, as the associations are highly transient due to their enzymatic nature51. We hypothesized that additional resolution and efficiency could be obtained in a subsequent μMap experiment under both native and perturbed ubiquitination, wherein we would have improved chances to preferentially identify key granule modulators specifically related to ubiquitin pathways.

We thus repeated our labeling workflow on HaloTag–G3BP1 stable cell lines with and without TAK-243 treatment throughout prestress and the entire disassembly process (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Data 3). TAK-243 inhibits global polyubiquitination across the proteome, and as anticipated, ubiquitin itself (RPS27A) was highly enriched only in (−)TAK-243 samples (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 3a–d), indicating successful capture of granule proteome differences triggered by TAK-243 ablation of polyubiquitination. Focusing on differentially enriched proteins related to ubiquitin pathways, we first searched for E3 ligases and identified several candidates enriched during AS in (+)TAK-243 cells (Fig. 3b,c and Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). Interestingly, all identified E3 ligases, including WWP2, ITCH, neuronal precursor cell-expressed developmentally downregulated 4 (NEDD4) and NEDD4L, belong to the HECT family, a distinct group that comprises ~28 members of over 600 total E3 ligases52. Differing from other ligase families that bridge ubiquitin transfer from E2 ligases to their substrates, HECT ligases instead covalently accept ubiquitin with a catalytic cysteine in their HECT domain followed by direct transfer to the substrate. Furthermore, all four candidates can be classified into the NEDD4 subfamily, all of which feature an N-terminal C2 membrane localization domain, several WW domains for substrate recognition and a characteristic C-terminal HECT domain (Extended Data Fig. 3e)53. HaloMap also identified their cognate adaptors, NDFIP1 and NDFIP2, in TAK-243-treated cells (Fig. 3b,c). Both proteins are known to activate HECT ligases and expand substrate recognition capabilities52, providing further evidence of HECT ligase activity regulating SG dynamics.

In addition to E3 ligases, we were interested in identifying proteins that may recognize ubiquitin PTMs and serve as adaptors for granule disassembly. Unlike E3-substrate recognition, which is not ubiquitin-dependent51,53, this ‘reader’ recognition requires active ubiquitination of specific granule substrates. In this regard, we investigated interactors in the absence of TAK-243 and identified a cluster of ubiquitin-binding proteins (Fig. 3b,d and Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). In particular, we observed the enrichment of valosin-containing protein (VCP), a transitional endoplasmic reticulum ATPase previously reported to regulate SG dynamics23,54,55. We also identified several ubiquitin receptors associated with autophagy, including SQSTM1, HDAC6 and TOLLIP, all of which have been shown to recognize polyubiquitinated substrates for autophagic targeting and degradation56. Known downstream autophagosome subunits, including GABARAPL2, HSPA8 and ATG9A, were also enriched in the absence of TAK-243, further implying the involvement of autophagy pathways in SG disassembly (Fig. 3b,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–d).

### HECT E3 ligases facilitate granule disassembly

Consistent enrichment of HECT E3 ligase members in our HaloMap experiment motivated us to study their functional impacts on SG dynamics. Although generally underexplored in their substrate scope, these ligases have been found to impact transforming growth factor β and PTEN signaling pathways, performing important roles in neuronal and immune cell development53. They have also been linked to many neurodegenerative diseases, regulating substrates that ostensibly engage in cytotoxic protein aggregates underlying Parkinson’s disease and ALS pathologies57. To investigate whether HECT E3 ligases have a role in SG disassembly, we treated cells with a HECT ligase-specific inhibitor, heclin58, throughout stress and recovery (Extended Data Fig. 3e). At 120 min recovery (D120), a substantial amount of granules remained in the heclin-treated samples, while untreated cells had fully cleared these condensates (Fig. 4a). We then repeated this experiment in a full kinetic analysis of granule clearance and observed that heclin-treated cells displayed ~2-h delays in clearance compared with untreated cells (Fig. 4b). HECT inhibition also had no impact on the initial formation of granules (Fig. 4b), consistent with our previous experiments using TAK-243 (Extended Data Fig. 2e). This heclin-dependent delay in granule disassembly was also consistent in both cancer cell line HeLa and neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y, suggesting a shared mechanism across different cell types and lineages (Extended Data Fig. 4a). In parallel, we also tested inhibition of the cullin–RING (really interesting new gene)-type E3 ligase family with the known NEDDylation inhibitor MLN4924, which had no measurable impact on granule kinetics as previously reported (Extended Data Fig. 4b)47, further supporting the specific influence of HECT ligases on granule disassembly.

We next explored whether specific HECT E3 ligases or their associated adaptors functionally regulate SG disassembly. To test this, we performed siRNA knockdown (KD) of each candidate protein identified in HaloMap (Fig. 3b,c), including all four ligases (WWP2, ITCH, NEDD4 and NEDD4L) and the two adaptors (NDFIP1 and NDFIP2). Individual KD of ITCH, NEDD4L and NDFIP1 led to measurable delays in SG disassembly in both HEK293 cells (Fig. 4c,d and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d) and neuronal SH-SY5Y cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e). However, combinatorial siRNA KD of these ligases did not exhibit a synergistic effect on granule disassembly, indicating possible redundancy in the regulation of granule kinetics by these homologous ligases (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Given that these ligases have not been previously associated with granules, we confirmed their subcellular localization via immunofluorescence against the granule marker G3BP1, observing their recruitment to SGs upon NaAsO2 treatment (Fig. 4e). Overexpression or siRNA KD of either ITCH or NEDD4L did not affect initial granule formation, again consistent with our results with both TAK-243 and heclin inhibition of polyubiquitination (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Together, these data indicate that specific HECT E3 ligases, including ITCH, NEDD4L and the associated adaptor protein NDFIP1, exert a direct regulatory role in ubiquitin-mediated SG disassembly.

We were next interested in determining more precise mechanisms surrounding HECT-dependent ubiquitination in granules and its role in governing disassembly rates. We initially used tandem ubiquitin-binding entities (TUBE) enrichment against pan-ubiquitin substrates to profile global ubiquitinome changes, comparing cells in the presence (+) or absence (−) of heclin during granule formation (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Data 4). GO analysis of the heclin-impacted ubiquitinome demonstrated functional enrichment of proteins involved in vesicle-mediated transport, regulation of K63-linked polyubiquitin chains and autophagy (Extended Data Fig. 5a). It is recognized that K48-linked ubiquitin PTMs commonly mark proteins for protease degradation, while the K63-linked PTMs tag proteins for autophagic clearance56. We then repeated this ubiquitinome profiling experiment but with K63-specific TUBE pulldown (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Data 5). Here we identified a set of 181 proteins, normally with increased K63-specific ubiquitination upon stress but now displaying substantially lower modification levels when cells were treated with heclin, among which 31 proteins are known SG components (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). GO analysis of these 181 targets also revealed strong associations with RNA metabolism, translation and cellular stress response (Extended Data Fig. 5b), characteristics mechanistically relevant to SG function. In line with this finding, immunofluorescence analysis revealed a decrease in the overlap of K63-specific ubiquitination signals within granule areas during heclin treatment, despite the continued formation of pan-ubiquitin-positive and K48-specific ubiquitin-positive granules (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 5d). Collectively, these data indicate that HECT E3 ligases modulate granule disassembly through the installation of K63-linked polyubiquitin chains on specific granule proteins. The absence of these modifications, resulting from compromised ligase activities, likely accounts for the delayed granule disassembly we observed when inhibiting this pathway.

### Ubiquitin receptor TOLLIP regulates granule disassembly

K63-specific polyubiquitin chains typically mark proteins for selective clearance through the autophagic pathway56. In this process, ubiquitin receptors ‘read’ these specific polyubiquitin PTMs on substrates and help to recruit phagophore subunits. Given our data implicating K63-linked polyubiquitin PTMs, we hypothesized that they facilitate the recruitment of certain ubiquitin receptors and downstream machinery, which could potentially disrupt the protein–protein interactions that sustain the phase-separated structure. Ubiquitin receptors VCP23,54, SQSTM1 and CALCOCO2 (ref. 59) have been reported to aid in granule disassembly, presumably through the recognition and extraction of specific granule scaffold proteins. Additionally, loss-of-function mutations in ubiquitin receptors, including VCP and SQSTM1, have been genetically associated with diseases like ALS through a potential condensate dysregulation mechanism14. Therefore, we were motivated to investigate the functional relationship of these ubiquitin receptors with granule clearance.

In our previous HaloMap analysis, we identified several ubiquitin receptors that were recruited to granules when cellular ubiquitination remained intact, including HDAC6, SQSTM1, TOLLIP and VCP (Fig. 3b,d). To elucidate their functional role in AS granule disassembly, we performed siRNA KD for all four identified proteins (Fig. 5a and Extended Data Fig. 6a). As expected, we observed no impact on SG formation with any of the KD conditions, yet TOLLIP KD resulted in a substantial delay in granule disassembly after 2-h recovery (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 6b). An extended kinetic evaluation of granule disassembly under TOLLIP KD manifested a more pronounced delay compared to heclin treatment, and even after 4 h of recovery, these cells still retained a substantial level of SGs (Fig. 5c). Combining heclin treatment with TOLLIP KD did not produce any additional inhibition in clearance, suggesting TOLLIP likely serves a more critical role in overall disassembly. TOLLIP is known to interact with ubiquitin-modified proteins through its CUE (coupling of ubiquitin to ER degradation) domain, in turn recruiting the autophagy-related proteins ATG8 or LC3 to promote autophagosome formation and protein turnover60. We confirmed colocalization of TOLLIP with SGs through immunofluorescence (Fig. 5d), and this recruitment was less apparent upon both heclin and TAK-243 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 6c), strongly suggesting interactions between TOLLIP and polyubiquitinated granule targets. Overall, these experiments identify TOLLIP as a new modulator of granule disassembly through a potential mechanism of recognizing the K63-ubiquitinated granule proteins and eventually leading to granule clearance.

### Autophagy mediates granule dynamics

TOLLIP is known to participate in autophagy, a central quality control system that recycles large subcellular components, including protein aggregates and organelles56. Autophagy degradation involves the receptor-mediated assembly of autophagosomes around ubiquitin-marked subcellular components followed by lysosomal fusion for digestion and recycling. There is ongoing debate about whether autophagy is directly involved in SG disassembly54,55,61. In our present study, we observe HaloMap enrichment of autophagy subunits (Fig. 3e), HECT E3 ligase-mediated K63-specific polyubiquitination of granule proteins (Fig. 4g,h) and the contribution of the autophagy-related ubiquitin receptor TOLLIP to granule disassembly (Fig. 5b,c), suggesting that autophagy machinery is likely involved in SG clearance.

To further test this hypothesis, we measured autophagy response during stress by detecting the truncation of LC3B, a widely used marker for autophagy activation56. The proportion of the activated LC3B-II isoform substantially increased upon AS, indicating a global autophagic activation in response to oxidative stress (Fig. 6a). Aligned with this finding, a high level of functional autophagosome formation was also detected in cells treated with NaAsO2 (Fig. 6b). These early autophagosomes likely interact with SGs as we observed their partial colocalization with SGs (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In addition, LC3B puncta structures were observed to colocalize with G3BP1/SG signals (Fig. 6c), suggesting possible regulatory involvement in SG clearance. We also pharmacologically inhibited autophagy using bafilomycin A1 (BafA1)62, which hinders autophagosome–lysosome fusion, and observed a measurable delay in SG disassembly compared to untreated cells (Fig. 6d). Finally, we explored whether pre-induced autophagy leads to faster granule clearance. We selected Torin 1 (ref. 63), a potent mTOR inhibitor, and TAT-D11 (ref. 64), a cell-permeable BECN1-activating peptide, to induce autophagy during pretreatment before oxidative stress. Induced autophagy resulted not only in smaller granule formation upon stress (Fig. 6e) but also a faster rate of clearance after 90 min recovery (D90), occurring roughly 30 min earlier than the approximate 2-h duration for granule disassembly under normal conditions (Fig. 6f). Together, these results underscore the role that autophagic machinery has in regulating SG kinetics, representing a potentially overlooked aspect in the understanding of SG disassembly.

## Discussion

Condensate biology has gained increasing research focus in recent years due to its relevance in both basic cellular processes and various disease pathologies2. Proper assembly and disassembly of phase-separated condensates are crucial to maintaining normal cellular function, and failure to recycle these droplets severely impairs overall metabolism, biomolecular trafficking, and homeostasis65. The dynamic organization of these phase-separated structures often relies on PTMs that alter protein conformations and induce new interactions19. These two properties comprise the hypothesized mechanism underlying age-dependent neurodegenerative diseases, such as ALS, where ubiquitin-positive cytotoxic inclusions often fail to be cleared in patient neurons14. Autophagy pathways are responsible for recycling larger cellular components and protein aggregates, and their functional integrity is frequently undermined in diseased cells, plausibly leading to the accumulation of these inclusions14,66.

Despite increasing research interest, it is difficult to study condensate dynamics using traditional biochemical methods, and the precise cellular mechanisms underlying both normal and disease-associated phase separation remain unclear. In this study, we introduce HaloMap as a photocatalytic proximity labeling approach to characterize intracellular protein networks. This chemogenetic approach combines the power of the Ir-based μMap platform with genetically encodable HaloTag technology to enable high-resolution proteome profiling in living cells. Here we apply HaloMap to profile the dynamic SG interactome in both time-resolved and pharmacologically modified contexts. From this protein interactome data, we were able to elucidate new roles for ubiquitin and ubiquitin-associated proteins in SG disassembly. Expanding on previous studies in this area23,24,48, our data support the hypothesis that ubiquitination is a key PTM required for SG disassembly and that these modifications likely occur during phase separation. By using HaloMap to compare granule proteomes both before and after ubiquitin inhibitor TAK-243 perturbation, we were able to capture the HECT E3 ubiquitin ligases ITCH and NEDD4L as well as the ligase adaptor NDFIP1, all three of which were shown to be required for efficient granule disassembly. Several questions remain from this study, particularly with respect to the exact granule protein substrates undergoing polyubiquitination by HECT ligase machinery. We hypothesize that these HECT ligases likely exhibit some redundancy as they contain similar substrate recognition domains. Additionally, the involvement of various adaptor proteins may augment substrate selectivity in other cellular contexts. Identifying precise substrates and understanding more mechanistic details surrounding HECT E3 ligase regulation will likely provide new insights into granule clearance machinery.

This study also underscores the functional involvement of autophagy pathways in the clearance of SGs. We specifically identified TOLLIP as a key autophagy-related granule modulator that likely recognizes ubiquitinated substrates to dismantle granular networks. As TOLLIP is also known to engage in the degradation of cytotoxic polyQ protein aggregates in Huntington’s disease67, our findings potentially suggest therapeutic targeting of this adaptor protein in other neurodegenerative diseases, in particular by designing agonists or recruiters of TOLLIP to resolve the malfunctioning cytosolic condensates. Finally, our experiments with the autophagy inducers Torin 1 and TAT-D11 demonstrated enhanced granule disassembly, offering further support to pharmacological approaches against neurodegeneration by upregulating autophagy pathways, a promising new direction aiming at boosting the recycling capability of aged cells against aggregates66,68.

Overall, this work not only provides a general chemogenetic proximity labeling method that can serve as a powerful tool for deciphering intracellular biology but also reveals several molecular mechanisms of SG disassembly to offer greater insights into condensate biology and therapeutic advances in neurodegenerative disease. We envision that the HaloMap method will be applicable to profiling a variety of intracellular interactomes. When combined with the specificity and temporal control of the μMap manifold36, this approach holds great promise in applications where achieving suborganelle resolution is key, presenting an exciting future for the exploration of complex intracellular interactions and dynamics.

## Methods

### Labeling reagents and pharmacological agents

Hexyl chloride–PEG4–Ir(G2) and biotin–PEG3–diazirine probes were prepared as previously reported39. NaAsO2 solution (0.1 N; Alfa Aesar, AA41533AP) was purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific. TAK-243 (HY-100487), heclin (HY-110204), Torin 1 (HY-13003) and BafA1 (HY-100558) were purchased from MedChemExpress. TAT-D11 peptide (NBP2-49888) was purchased from Novus Biologicals.

### Primary antibodies

All the following antibodies were used for immunofluorescence: rabbit anti-G3BP1 (Cell Signaling Technology, 61559S; 1:200), mouse anti-G3BP1 (Proteintech, 66486-1-Ig; 1:500), mouse anti-G3BP1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-365338; 1:200), rabbit anti-HaloTag (Promega, G928A; 1:1,000), rabbit anti-PDIA6 (Abcam, ab154820; 1:100), rabbit anti-PUM3 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA002353; 1:200), rabbit anti-RPL4 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA034600; 1:200), mouse anti-pan-ubiquitin (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8017; 1:200), mouse anti-HA-tag (Invitrogen, 26183; 1:500), rabbit anti-K63-ubiquitin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA532573; 1:200), rabbit anti-K48-ubiquitin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA535382; 1:200), rabbit anti-TOLLIP (Proteintech, 11315-1-AP; 1:200) and rabbit anti-LC3B (Cell Signaling Technology, 3868S; 1:200).

### Generation of stable cell lines

To generate stable cell lines expressing HaloTag–G3BP1 and HaloTag–NES, Flp-In T-Rex 293 cells were seeded in six-well plates and cotransfected with pOG44 (2 μg; Invitrogen, V600520), pcDNA5-FRT-HaloTag-G3BP1 or pcDNA5-FRT-HaloTag-NES (0.2 μg) using FuGENE HD (Promega, E2311) transfection reagent following the vendor’s protocol. An additional supplement of 200 μg ml−1 hygromycin B (Gibco, 10687010) was used for the selection and maintenance of each stable cell line. Expression of fusion proteins was confirmed with immunofluorescence microscopy and western blot.

### SG formation and disassembly

To trigger SG formation, a solution of 500 μM NaAsO2 in complete DMEM was applied to cells for 30 min. To disassemble NaAsO2-induced SGs, cells were rinsed twice with fresh DMEM to remove the stressor and then left to recover for the indicated time at 37 °C, 5% CO2. During recovery, the media was changed every 30 min. Additional drug treatment required pre-incubation before stressing and was maintained throughout recovery unless specifically noted (TAK-243–2 μM, 1-h pre-incubation; heclin–25 μM, 1-h pre-incubation; BafA1–100 nM, 3-h pre-incubation; Torin 1–250 nM, 9-h pre-incubation and TAT-D11–10 μM, 9-h pre-incubation).

### Proximity labeling workflow

Stable cell lines were seeded into poly-l-lysine-coated (EMD Millipore, A-005-C) 10-cm dishes with three biological replicates for each condition and grown to 95% confluency on the day of labeling. Cells were first incubated with complete DMEM media containing 5 μM Ir ligand for 1 h, followed by 4× 30 min wash with complete DMEM media to remove unbound Ir. For native state interactome labeling, cells were then incubated with 500 μM biotin–diazirine in complete FluoroBrite DMEM without Phenol Red (Gibco, A1896701) for 30 min. For stressed state labeling, 500 μM NaAsO2 was co-incubated with biotin–diazirine for 30 min in complete FluoroBrite DMEM without phenol red. For labeling of disassembly stages, cells were stressed and recovered in complete DMEM until switching to probe-containing complete FluoroBrite DMEM media 30 min before photolabeling. For labeling of all time points with TAK-243, 2 μM TAK-243 was predosed starting 1 h after Ir incubation and maintained throughout the entire experiment (versus DMSO vehicle control). After biotin–diazirine incubation, cells were directly subjected to 10-min irradiation with M2 photoreactors (Acceled; outfitted with a 450 nm LED plate, 100% intensity, corresponding to an output of 2.2 W). Finally, cells were collected, washed with cold DPBS (Dulbecco’s phosphate buffered saline) buffer (Gibco, 14190136), pelleted and stored at −80 °C for future use. The cell lysate was generated by resuspending cells in RIPA (radioimmunoprecipitation assay) lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 89901), briefly sonicating with a dismembrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, FB505) to lyse cells and clarifying at 15,000g for 15 min. Supernatants were transferred into separate tubes, and the protein concentration was quantified with BCA (bicinchoninic acid) assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23227) with a BioTek Gen5 v2.05 plate reader.

### Pulldown enrichment for label-free proteomics and western blotting

To enrich HaloMap-tagged proteins for label-free proteomics, normalized 0.5 mg cell lysate per replicate was incubated with 50 μl Pierce Streptavidin Beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88816) pre-equilibrated in RIPA in Eppendorf Protein LoBind tubes (Z666505) and incubated at 4°C overnight. The next day, samples were reduced on beads via a supplement of 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; Millipore-Sigma, 3860) for 30 min at room temperature, followed by cysteine alkylation with 15 mM indole-3-acetic acid (IAA; Sigma-Aldrich, I6125) for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. IAA was then quenched with DTT (20 mM final concentration) for 15 min at room temperature. Samples were then washed 3× with 1% SDS in DPBS, 3× with 1 M NaCl in DPBS and 3× with 10% EtOH in DPBS. Finally, samples were washed 3× with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (Sigma-Aldrich, 09830) buffer and resuspended in 30 μl 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer containing 0.5 μg MS-grade trypsin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 90057) per sample and digested at 37 °C overnight with rotation. Trypsin was then quenched with 1 μl Optima LC–MS formic acid (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A117-50), and supernatants were passed through a 0.22-μm spin filter column (CoStar, 98231-UT-1) before being transferred to an LC–MS vial for proteomics analysis. To enrich HaloMap-labeled proteins for western blot validation, 0.5 mg cell lysate was incubated with streptavidin beads as described earlier, followed by a series of sequential washes–3× with 1% SDS in DPBS, 3× with 1 M NaCl in DPBS and 3× with 10% EtOH in DPBS. Beads were finally resuspended in DPBS in new LoBind tubes, pelleted and incubated with 30 μl freshly made elution buffer (30 mM biotin, 6 M urea, 2 M thiourea, 2% SDS in DPBS and 20% 4× Laemmli with BME (pH 11.5)) and heated to 95 °C for 15 min with 1,000 rpm shaking. Supernatants were collected while hot and cooled to room temperature before western blot loading.

### MS-based proteomics and data analysis

Label-free, data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics was performed on a Bruker TimsTOF Pro 2 connected to a nanoElute LC. For each sample, ~100 ng of protein was injected onto a trap column (C18 Pepmap; 5 μM particle size, 5 mm length and 300 μM internal diameter), followed by separation via an analytical column (C18 ReproSil AQ; 1.9 μM particle size, 100 mm length and 75 μM internal diameter). Peptides were eluted via an acetonitrile/water gradient at a column temperature of 40 °C (buffer A = 0.1% formic acid/water, buffer B = 0.1% formic acid/acetonitrile; flow rate = 0.5 μl min−1; gradient–start at 2% buffer B, then increase to 35% buffer B over 20 min, increase to 95% buffer B over 0.5 min, hold at 95% for 2.25 min). Scans were performed in positive ion, dia-PASEF (parallel accumulation serial fragmentation) mode over a m/z range of 100–1,700 with a ramp time of 100 ms, accumulation time of 100 ms and a duty cycle of 100%, ramp rate of 9.43 Hz, MS averaging set to 1. Absolute thresholds were set to 5,000 for mobility peaks and 10 for MS peaks. Data were collected with Bruker Compass HyStar v.6.2.

The resulting raw data (.d files) were then processed via DIA-NN 1.8.1 (refs. 69,70) via the following parameters: trypsin/P digestion, three missed cleavages, three maximum variable modifications, N-term M excision, Ox(M), Ac(N-term) and C-carbamidomethylation, peptide length range of 7–30, precursor charge range 1–4, m/z range 300–1,800, fragment ion range 200–1,800, mass accuracy and MS accuracy both set to 10, precursor false discovery rate set to 1%. Within the DIA-NN algorithm, the following settings are applied: ‘use isotopologues’, ‘MBR’ (match between runs), ‘no shared spectra’ and ‘heuristic protein inference’. A spectral library was used, which was generated in DIA-NN from all known human proteins (in silico spectral library–generated in DIA-NN via FASTA of Uniprot human proteome UP000005640–options selected were ‘FASTA digest for library-free search/library generation’ and ‘deep learning-based spectra, retention times and ion mobilities prediction’, other parameters same as described above). After processing, the resulting matrix.pg files were worked up in Perseus (v.2.0.7.0)71, where intensities are inputted as ‘main’, while the other descriptors are listed as ‘categorical’. Intensities were transformed by log2, and data were annotated to the appropriate condition (for example, prestress and D30). At this point, missing values were replaced from a normal distribution (width = 0.3, downshift = 1.8, separately for each column). Normalization was performed via median subtraction, and a volcano plot was generated using a t-test for statistical significance. Resulting volcano plots were plotted in GraphPad Prism 9.5 for final figures. Heatmaps and balloon plots were further plotted based on Perseus-processed output protein intensities and using Morpheus online tools (https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus) with selected protein sets as noted specifically. Protein clustering was performed using a standard tool in Morpheus. GO analysis was performed on Metascape v.3.5 (ref. 72).

### Immunofluorescence microscopy and processing

Cells were seeded into poly-l-lysine-coated (EMD Millipore, A-005-C) glass-bottom chamber slides (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 155409; eight-well chamber slide) or plates (Cellvis, 230224; 24-well plate; Cellvis, 221222; 96-well plate) and grown to 90% confluency. Following the appropriate stress and/or labeling, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in DPBS for 15 min at room temperature, washed once with DPBS and then permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 in DPBS for 10 min. Samples were then incubated at room temperature for 1 h in blocking buffer (3% BSA and 0.05% Tween 20 in DPBS). A primary antibody solution was then prepared in blocking buffer and applied for at least 1 h at room temperature or overnight at 4 °C. Samples were then washed 3× with 0.05% Tween 20 in DPBS and stained with a secondary antibody solution in blocking buffer for 1 h at room temperature. Hoechst 33342 (Tocris Bioscience, 5117; 1:10,000) was used for nuclear staining. Goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, A32731; 1:1000), goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 488 (Invitrogen, A11001; 1:1,000), goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 555 (Invitrogen, A21428; 1:1,000) and goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 555 (Invitrogen, A21422; 1:1,000) were used to target specific primary antibodies. Streptavidin Alexa Fluor 555 (Invitrogen, S21381; 1:2,000) was used for detecting biotinylation. Finally, samples were washed 3×0.05% Tween 20 in DPBS and stored in DPBS before imaging. CYTO-ID autophagy detection reagent (Enzo Life Sciences, 501031812) was used for autophagosome staining 30 min before cell fixation. Samples were imaged using NIS Elements AR v4.60.00 software on a Nikon A1R-Si HD confocal microscope.

Image processing and quantification were performed with ImageJ2/FIJI Mac OS X software. For image replicates at different conditions, SG areas and cytosolic areas were analyzed using threshold-combined area measurement for individual pictures. SG sizes were measured using threshold-combined particle analyzing tools. Line profile plots were analyzed using the plot profile function based on the line drawing across the granules. Gray values/intensity were normalized based on the maximal intensity within each channel. All quantification results were further plotted with Prism 9.5.

### Western blotting

Lysate samples were prepared with normalized concentration (20–50 μg). Electrophoresis was performed on a 4–15% gradient Criterion TGX Precast Midi Protein Gel (Bio-Rad, 5671048). Gels were then transferred against 0.45 μm nitrocellulose membranes (Bio-Rad, 1620115). Membranes were then washed with 0.05% Tween 20 in tris-buffered saline (TBST) and blocked for 1 h at room temperature in 3% BSA in TBST. Primary antibody was then prepared in blocking buffer and applied to the membrane overnight at 4 °C with gentle agitation. Membranes were then washed 3× with TBST and incubated with a secondary antibody solution (1:10,000) in a blocking buffer for at least 1 h at room temperature. Secondary antibodies used in this study, where appropriate—IRDye 680RD goat anti-mouse (LI-COR, 926-68070), IRDye 680RD goat anti-rabbit (LI-COR, 926-68071), IRDye 800CW goat anti-mouse (LI-COR, 926-32210), IRDye 800CW goat anti-rabbit (LI-COR, 926-32211) and IRDye 800CW streptavidin (LI-COR, 926-32230). Afterward, the buffer was decanted, and the membranes were washed 3× with TBST and water before imaging with an Image Studio v5.2 software on LI-COR Odyssey CLx scanner in the 700 nm and 800 nm channels.

### Transient transfection

Cells were seeded for overnight recovery before transient transfection for protein expression. A 100 μl transfection mixture was prepared in OPTI-MEM media (Gibco, 14190136) with 2 μg of plasmid and 6 μl of FuGENE HD reagent following standard protocol. For each well of cells in 6-well plates, 24-well plates, 96-well plates and 8-chamber slides, 50 μl, 15 μl, 6 μl and 10 μl of the transfection mixture were added to cells in complete DMEM media, respectively. Media was replaced the next day, and cells were left to recover for 24 h before subsequent experiments or analysis.

### TUBE pulldown and proteomics

For TUBE pulldown proteomics, the following products were used from LifeSensors: UM404M-1000 for K63-specific ubiquitination and UM-0402M-1000 for pan-ubiquitination studies. Cells were grown to confluency and subjected to stress conditions as described above. Cells were lysed with RIPA buffer containing protease inhibitor and 50 μM PR-619 DUB inhibitor. Upon lysis, 50 μl of the corresponding magnetic TUBE beads were loaded with 500 μg of lysate and incubated at 4 °C overnight. The following proteomics preparation is similar to that used above for streptavidin enrichment. After binding, proteins on beads were reduced via DTT, followed by alkylation with IAA, which was then quenched with additional DTT. Following reduction and alkylation, beads were washed 3× with TBST, followed by three washes with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer. Proteins were digested from beads with 0.5 μg MS-grade trypsin in 40 μl of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer (in Optima grade water). After trypsin quenching with optima-grade formic acid, samples were filtered via a 0.22-micron spin filter before proceeding to proteomics.

### Cell viability assay

Cells were seeded on poly-l-lysine-coated 96-well plates and recovered overnight. The RealTime-Glo MT Cell Viability Assay Kit (Promega, G9711) was used for measuring cell survival rate during incubation. The 2× reaction mixture was prepared by combining the MT Cell Viability Substrate with NanoLuc Enzyme in complete DMEM media, and 50 μl of the mixture was distributed to each well. Then, 50 μl 2× serial dilutions of the Ir–PEG4–hexyl chloride (100 μM to 0.391 μM) in complete DMEM were added to each well in biological triplicates. Control samples were dosed with DMSO. Cells were continuously incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2 atmosphere, and the luminescence was read over time using a BioTek Gen5 v2.05 plate reader with the following settings: luminescence, optical fiber and 135 gain. Cell viability was calculated according to the luminescence intensities.

### Live-cell confocal imaging

Cells were seeded on poly-l-lysine-coated glass-bottom chamber slides (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 155379; Nunc Lab-Tek II 2-well chamber slide) and grown to 70% confluency. One day before imaging, the media was changed to fresh, complete DMEM containing 1,000-fold diluted HaloTag TMRDirect ligand (Promega, G2991) and incubated overnight. The excess ligand was washed away with complete FluoroBrite DMEM (Gibco, A1896701) for 30 min before imaging. Samples were incubated in an environmental control chamber at 37 °C and 5% CO2 atmosphere during the entire imaging process. A Nikon Ti-E spinning disk confocal microscope was used for live-cell imaging. Pictures were taken at intervals of 5 min to minimize phototoxicity. Multiple xy parameters were preset for the automated imaging system to acquire different cell images within one chamber as technical replicates. For each field, pictures were taken at multiple z stacks to better capture granule dynamics within cells. Image processing, quantification and video production were performed with ImageJ2/FIJI software. Maximum projection was used to consolidate z-stack images at each time point. SGs and cytosolic area were analyzed using threshold-combined measurements for consolidated pictures.

### Statistical analysis and reproducibility

Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 9.5. Comparisons between the two means were performed by two-tailed Student’s t-test. Comparisons among multiple means were performed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s test. Experiments with technical replicates (Figs. 1, 2 and 4–6 and Extended Data Figs. 1, 4 and 6), biological replicates (Figs. 1–6 and Extended Data Figs. 1, 2 and 4) and independent repeats (Figs. 1, 2 and 4–6 and Extended Data Figs. 1, 4 and 6) are stated in figure legends.
